readerTitle: The orange trucks stay: a rebrand decision, step by step
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (목재 크레이트 제조·물류 회사, 이후 B2B 컨설팅 서비스로 확장) · 모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용
insight: 리브랜딩은 다시 시작하는 일이 아니라 고치는 일이다. 고객이 우리를 알아보고 믿는 데 쓰는 것은 지키고, 고객을 막고 있는 것만 바꾼다.
misconception: 브랜드가 낡아 보이면 이름과 로고를 새로 바꾸는 것이 곧 브랜드를 강하게 만드는 길이다.

sources.text: Romaniuk, J. (2018). Building Distinctive Brand Assets. Oxford University Press. (독특한 브랜드 자산 개념)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 회사(Harlow Crate & Freight), 인물(Dana), 에이전시 견적 $60,000, 트럭 14대, 고객 인터뷰 15명은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 사례처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
Romaniuk(2018) 책의 서지 정보(출판사, 연도)를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 본문에는 책의 수치나 인용을 쓰지 않았습니다.
리브랜딩이 타당한 경우(오해를 부르는 이름, 합병, 상표 분쟁, 스캔들)는 일반론으로만 적었습니다. 특정 국가의 상표법 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The trucks are orange. The logo is from 1987.
body: Dana just took over Harlow Crate & Freight from her father. The firm makes wooden crates and pallets, stores goods and delivers them across the region.
An agency has pitched a fresh start: a new name, *Nexora Logistics*, a cool teal look, and a $60,000 quote. Dana is tempted. The old logo does look tired.
Over the next few cards, you make her calls.

image.label: An orange delivery truck with an old-fashioned logo beside a stack of crates
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 오래된 서체 로고가 붙은 주황색 배송 트럭과, 옆면에 'H' 낙인이 찍힌 나무 크레이트 더미. 한쪽 구석에 청록색 새 로고 시안이 놓인 테이블. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where do you start?
body: Dana has a budget, an eager agency and a feeling that the brand is holding the firm back. She doesn't yet know why, or if that's true.

options.text: Hire the agency. A modern look will win bigger clients
options.feedback: You'd spend $60,000 fixing a problem nobody has confirmed, and you might erase things customers rely on without knowing it.

options.text: Talk to 15 customers and a few lost prospects: why they pick you, what they remember
options.feedback: A brand is what's in customers' heads, not on the letterhead. A few weeks of listening tells you what to protect and what to fix.

options.text: Ask the staff to vote on the agency's new logo designs
options.feedback: Staff buy-in matters, but staff aren't the buyers. Liking a logo says little about why anyone signs a contract.

cards.title: Say you chose to listen. Here's what you heard.
body: Customers say the same things: "They're never late." Warehouse staff spot the orange trucks from across the yard. Buyers know the stamped **H** on every pallet.
But two lost prospects thought Harlow only made crates. They had no idea it also stores and delivers. What do you change?

options.text: New name and a new color, to look like a real logistics company
options.feedback: It signals logistics, but it throws away the orange and the H that people use to recognize you. You'd rebuild recognition from zero.

options.text: Keep the orange and the H, tidy the lettering, add a line: Crates · Storage · Delivery
options.feedback: You fix the real gap, which is what prospects don't know, while keeping the cues customers already use to find you.

options.text: Change nothing. The old look clearly works
options.feedback: You keep all your recognition, but the actual problem stays: new buyers still don't know half of what you sell.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the same cues are the app icon, color and product name users scan for on a crowded screen. Redesign the icon completely and some loyal users may struggle to find the app they open every day.

cards.title: Say you kept the orange and the H. Now roll it out.
body: Harlow has 14 trucks, thousands of crates in circulation, and invoices that big customers' accounts teams process every month.
How do you introduce the refreshed look?

options.text: Repaint all 14 trucks in one week and host a launch event
options.feedback: It makes a splash, but trucks off the road risk late deliveries, the one thing you're known for never doing.

options.text: Update the website, invoices and signs now, repaint trucks at their regular service, and tell key customers first what changes and what doesn't
options.feedback: The change costs less, keeps deliveries on time, and customers hear "same people, same promise" before they see anything new.

options.text: Switch quietly. No announcement, no fuss
options.feedback: An invoice with a new look and no warning can make a customer wonder if the firm was sold, or flag it as possible fraud.

cards.title: Say you rolled it out in steps. Then a client asks for advice.
body: Six months later, a food producer asks Harlow to redesign its packaging and loading plans to cut damage in transit. Dana sees a new business: paid packaging and load planning for clients.
This is a professional service, not a product. What do you call it?

options.text: A separate, stylish name so it feels like a real consultancy
options.feedback: It may look polished, but you'd ask buyers to trust an adviser they've never heard of, and you'd split your marketing effort in two.

options.text: Harlow Load Planning, sold on the same promise: on time, no surprises
options.feedback: The trust Harlow has earned carries over. The catch: the service must keep that promise, or it weakens the whole brand.

options.text: Partner with a known consultancy and sell under its name
options.feedback: You borrow instant credibility, but the partner owns the client relationship and the reputation you build.

cards.title: A rebrand is a repair, not a restart.
body: Dana spent far less than $60,000 and lost none of the recognition the firm had built over decades. The new line fixed the one thing blocking new buyers.

breakdown.label: Orange, the H mark, the name
breakdown.detail: How customers spot and remember Harlow

breakdown.label: Crates · Storage · Delivery
breakdown.detail: Tells prospects what the firm does

cards.callout: Fix what blocks customers. Keep what they already use to find and trust you.
cards.softwareNote: A software company can face the same test when it adds products. A clear product line under a familiar name often does what a whole new brand promises, for far less.

cards.title: Sometimes a bigger change is the right call.
body: A full rebrand can make sense when the name actively misleads buyers, after a merger, when someone else owns the rights to your name, or when the brand is tied to a scandal.
Even then, budget for a long stretch where people don't recognize you. Carry over any cue you safely can.
And 15 interviews is a small sample. Listen for patterns that repeat, not for votes.

cards.title: Before you change your brand, find out what it already is.
body: Each of Dana's calls used one idea from this unit:
list: **Listen first:** a brand lives in customers' heads (*What a brand is*)
**Keep the orange and the H:** protect cues people use to find you (*Distinctive assets*)
**Roll out in steps, tell customers:** change without breaking trust (*Brand trust*, *Consistency*)
**Sell advice under the same name:** extend only what you can keep (*The brand promise*)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** ask three customers what they remember about your business. Write down every word, color or symbol they mention before you touch any of it.
